stories.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday he will run for Senate majority leader against Chuck Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017. Sen. stories.background: Democrats won control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which means their caucus leader will become majority leader when the new Congress is seated. Chuck Schumer of New York has held the top Democratic post in the Senate since 2017. Senate Democrats pick their leader in a private vote among themselves. Questions about Schumer's future had been building for some time; Semafor reported in December 2025 that Senate Democrats had put off the leadership debate until after the midterms. stories.headline: ICE reports record arrests and deportations for fiscal 2026
stories.summary: Immigration and Customs Enforcement said it arrested and deported more people in the past fiscal year than in any year of its 23-year history. Hegseth, a former Army National Guard officer, has led the Pentagon since January 2025.

stories.headline: Europe to join next round of Ukraine peace talks as Putin holds to his demands
stories.summary: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin on Thursday, then flew to Dublin to see Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky and Kushner said European countries will take part in the next round of talks with Russia, and Zelensky said a prisoner exchange is coming that would be the largest yet. Putin indicated Russia would not compromise on its core demands, and European governments have not yet agreed on who will speak for them.
stories.why_it_matters: The war is close to five years old, and who sits at the table shapes any deal on borders, troops and security guarantees that would affect all of Europe. Meanwhile fighting continues, with Ukraine saying limits on a U.S. satellite service are making it harder to stop Russian drones.
stories.background: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The Trump administration has been running talks through envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president's son-in-law, with earlier rounds held in Abu Dhabi. European governments, which supply much of Ukraine's aid, have pressed for a seat in those talks, and Ukraine has wanted them there because it is wary of leaving negotiations to Washington alone. Leaders of more than 40 European countries were meeting in Dublin this week for a summit on the continent's security. Separately, Ukraine's military relies on Starshield, a satellite communications service from Elon Musk's SpaceX, and has reported restrictions on it twice.

stories.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza's Nasser Hospital kills six, health officials say
stories.summary: An Israeli airstrike on the Nasser Hospital complex in southern Gaza this week killed six people, including a doctor and a child, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. Israel's military said it was targeting Hamas militants and that Hamas had set up a command center at the site; Hamas called the strike a crime against a civilian medical facility. The Board of Peace said the strike showed the need to move ahead with the peace plan.
stories.why_it_matters: The strike came during a ceasefire and hit a major hospital in a health system the AP describes as devastated, raising doubts about whether the truce and the stalled U.S.-backed peace plan will hold. Coverage in the digest comes mostly from left-leaning and center outlets.
stories.background: Nasser Hospital, in the southern city of Khan Younis, is one of Gaza's main medical centers and has been hit before during the war between Israel and Hamas. A ceasefire is in place under a peace plan promoted by President Trump, with a body called the Board of Peace attached to it, but The Wall Street Journal reported that progress on the plan has stalled. Casualty figures in Gaza come from the Health Ministry, which is run by Hamas. Israel has repeatedly said Hamas uses hospitals for military purposes, which Hamas denies.

stories.headline: Iran reports tanker explosions in Strait of Hormuz and says it hit a U.S. radar in Bahrain
stories.summary: Iran said explosions damaged oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday and that a tanker carrying liquefied natural gas hit a mine on Friday. Iran's Revolutionary Guard also said it targeted a U.S. early-warning radar in Bahrain, and Yemen's Houthis said they attacked a Saudi oil pipeline. These are claims by the groups involved; the reports reviewed carry no U.S. confirmation of the radar strike.
stories.why_it_matters: About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so attacks on tankers there can push up fuel prices everywhere. Coverage in the digest comes almost entirely from center-rated outlets and wire services.
stories.background: The United States and Israel have been at war with Iran, and Iran moved to block the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula used by Gulf oil exporters. The Hindu reports that tanker traffic has rebounded and oil prices have fallen on expectations the conflict will ease, but ships are still being hit. The U.S. Navy is blockading Iranian ports. Saudi Arabia has leaned more on its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to get oil out without using the strait. The Houthis are an Iran-aligned armed group that controls much of Yemen.

Saudi Arabia is pressing the European Union to designate the Houthis a terrorist group, Reuters reported.

stories.headline: Indonesia's vice president resigns after courts reject his education documents
stories.summary: Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Indonesia's 39-year-old vice president and the son of former President Joko Widodo, has resigned amid questions about his eligibility for office. Two top courts ruled last month that the documents he submitted about his overseas education did not meet election requirements. He had told President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday that he intended to step down, according to Indonesian media.
stories.why_it_matters: Indonesia is the world's fourth most populous country and its largest Muslim-majority democracy; the resignation removes the figure who tied the current president to his popular predecessor. For Indonesians it is a test of whether election rules apply to powerful families.
stories.background: Gibran is the eldest son of Joko Widodo, known as Jokowi, who was president from 2014 to 2024. He ran as Prabowo Subianto's running mate in the 2024 election, and The New York Times describes him as a symbol of the partnership that brought Prabowo to office. His eligibility has been challenged over the schooling he completed abroad. Last month the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled that his education documents fell short of what candidates must provide. Indonesian outlets reported that lawmakers were also preparing a parliamentary motion on his eligibility.

stories.headline: Pope Leo meets abuse victims in Peru and returns to the city where he was bishop
stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV met six victims of clerical abuse in Peru on Thursday and said the Catholic Church must make amends to survivors. In the same visit he denounced a culture of 'machismo' and called for women and girls to be protected. On Friday he was due to celebrate an outdoor Mass in Chiclayo, the northern city where he served as bishop for eight years.
stories.why_it_matters: The pope leads about 1.4 billion Catholics, and what he says on abuse and on violence against women sets direction for church leaders worldwide. Reuters reports he is weighing changes to how the Church treats abuse victims.
stories.background: Leo XIV, born in the United States, spent decades in Peru as a missionary and later as bishop of Chiclayo before his election as pope in 2025. The Peru stop is part of a 12-day South America tour, and the Chiclayo Mass is its centerpiece. Peru's Catholic Church was shaken by abuse within Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, a lay movement that the Vatican has since disbanded. The AP reported in 2025 that victims of that group said the future pope helped them when others did not.

stories.headline: Dutch prime minister holds crisis talks to save coalition after tax deal dispute
stories.summary: Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten called his coalition partners to crisis talks on Friday after one of the governing parties objected to a tax deal struck with the opposition. Jetten conceded the coalition needs a 'serious fresh start'. If the talks fail, the Netherlands could face a snap election.
stories.why_it_matters: A collapse would leave one of the eurozone's largest economies without a working government during budget season and could send Dutch voters back to the polls. The dispute is over how wealth and income are taxed, which affects household finances directly.
stories.background: Rob Jetten leads a minority government of three parties that together hold 66 of the 150 seats in the lower house of parliament, so it needs opposition votes to pass anything. DutchNews identifies the partners as Jetten's D66, the Christian Democrat CDA and the right-leaning liberal VVD. Budget and tax talks with opposition parties have dragged on for weeks. DutchNews reported on Nov. 5 that D66 and CDA were ready to back opposition tax amendments even if the VVD voted against them. Reuters describes the current dispute as a row over a wealth tax.

stories.summary: Taiwanese officials told Reuters that China has carried out military drills in the Pacific without announcing them, a tactic they called 'silent intimidation'. Taiwanese officials say the latest drills were held without any announcement from Beijing.

stories.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigns; CFO Colette Kress steps in as investors weigh the AI trade
stories.summary: Nvidia said Thursday that co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive and board member, effective immediately, after news reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects of spying for China. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Thursday, according to France 24, and investors now turn to the company's earnings next week.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable companies and a large part of many index funds and retirement accounts, so a change at the top can move ordinary savers' balances. Its chips also sit at the center of the AI spending that has been driving the stock market.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the processors that power most AI data centers, and Huang co-founded the company and led it until this week. On Nov. 8 the board said it was opening an independent investigation after reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and said then that it had confidence in him. Outlets including the BBC, The Hindu and The Hill have since reported allegations of extramarital affairs, one involving a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy; Huang admitted being unfaithful to his wife but did not give details, The Hindu reported. Kress, a 13-year Nvidia veteran, has been its finance chief. The company is due to report earnings next week, the same week as a planned Anthropic stock listing, according to The Wall Street Journal and Reuters.

facts.text: Nvidia said in a securities filing dated Nov. 12 that Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while keeping her finance role, and the board said it will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.
The board named director Harvey C. Jones as its first chair, according to the filing.
On Nov. 8 the board said it was opening an independent investigation after reporting that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and said it had confidence in him.
The resignation followed news reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of spying for China, according to the BBC, France 24 and CNBC.
Huang admitted being unfaithful to his wife but did not disclose details of the alleged relationship with the woman suspected of spying, The Hindu reported.
Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% on Thursday, France 24 reported; CNBC said the stock edged higher early Friday.
Other AI stocks pared their losses on Thursday, Reuters reported, and world shares posted modest losses on Friday, according to the Associated Press.
The BBC reported that Huang has been summoned to testify before Congress, and The Japan Times reported that Congress is stepping up scrutiny of both Nvidia and President Trump.

The New York Times reported that Trump was told of the suspicions last year and that he called Huang and urged him to fight for his job, according to The Japan Times and The Hill, which cited the Times.
Singapore said it had barred the woman at the center of the spying allegations from re-entering the country and that U.S. authorities gave limited help with its investigations, CNBC reported.
Some Nvidia staff in China were stunned by the exit, which raised questions about the company's operations there, the South China Morning Post reported, citing company sources.
Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's planned stock listing next week are seen as two tests for AI stocks, according to The Wall Street Journal and Reuters.

stories.headline: Fed officials signal more rate increases as inflation runs hot and bond yields jump
stories.summary: Federal Reserve officials said this week that inflation is still too high, with New York Fed president John Williams saying the central bank has "work to do." Treasury yields posted their biggest surge since 2022 as traders bet on more rate increases, MarketWatch reported, and bitcoin fell below $70,000. The Fed also said its October 2027 meeting will be a strategy session with no vote on interest rates.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher Fed rates and Treasury yields feed into what people pay on mortgages, car loans and credit cards. They also tend to weigh on stock and crypto prices.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve sets short-term interest rates to keep inflation near 2%. Officials had expected to cut rates this year but are instead preparing for another fight against inflation, CNBC reported, after a higher-than-expected October reading. Axios reported that price increases have spread beyond a few categories and tied the pressure to the Iran war and tariffs. Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, is also changing how the central bank operates and communicates, according to The New York Times and MarketWatch.

facts.text: New York Fed president John Williams said the central bank has "work to do" to bring inflation back to its target, Reuters reported.
San Francisco Fed president Mary Daly said the Fed has time to calibrate its rate increases, according to Reuters.

Bond yields had their biggest surge since 2022 as expectations grew for more Fed rate increases, MarketWatch reported.
Longer-dated Treasurys kept selling off on Friday and stock futures fell, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Bitcoin fell below $70,000 for the first time since August and was headed for a sixth straight weekly loss, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing expectations of higher rates and the tech selloff.
The Fed said its October 2027 meeting will not include a vote on interest rates or a post-meeting statement, leaving seven voting meetings next year, according to CNBC and The New York Times.
Some Fed officials are questioning whether raising rates gradually will be enough to contain inflation, Axios reported.

stories.headline: Oil market swings back to surplus as Gulf exports recover, IEA says
stories.summary: The International Energy Agency said Friday that the global oil market is moving into a supply surplus for the first time since the start of the Iran war, as Persian Gulf exports recover despite the continuing conflict. The agency cautioned that rebuilding depleted stockpiles will take months, the Financial Times reported. European stock indexes turned positive as oil prices dropped, according to The Wall Street Journal.
stories.why_it_matters: More oil supply tends to lower prices for gasoline, heating and shipping, which would ease one source of the inflation the Fed is trying to bring down.
stories.background: The International Energy Agency, a Paris-based body that advises oil-consuming countries, publishes a monthly report on supply and demand. The Iran war disrupted shipping from the Persian Gulf, a main source of the world's crude, and drained stockpiles. In its October report the agency said Gulf crude exports had climbed to more than 75% of pre-war levels in September as producers used routes that avoid the Strait of Hormuz, while fuel markets stayed tight.

stories.headline: City Council passes ban on 'surveillance pricing' based on shoppers' personal data
stories.summary: The City Council voted Thursday to prohibit surveillance pricing, the practice of using a customer's personal or browsing data to charge that person a different price for the same product. Speaker Julie Menin sponsored the bill and rejected objections from companies including Uber. The bill now goes to the mayor.
stories.why_it_matters: If it becomes law, businesses selling to New Yorkers could not quote you a higher price than your neighbor because of what your data says about you.
stories.background: Surveillance pricing means setting an individual price for a shopper using data about that person, such as browsing history. Menin and Majority Leader Shaun Abreu introduced a bill on it, Intro 891, in May, and a Council committee held a hearing in June. The Partnership for New York City, a business group, urged the Council not to act, arguing that a state bill already covers the practice; state lawmakers voted in June for their own ban. A bill passed by the Council goes to the mayor, who can sign it, veto it or let it become law without a signature.

stories.headline: State audit finds city's juvenile detention centers far over capacity as overtime quadruples
stories.summary: A new state audit found that New York City's two juvenile detention centers are holding far more young people than they were built for, THE CITY reported. Staff overtime has quadrupled and the average stay has nearly doubled, according to the audit. It also found the number of probation officers fell by a third since 2020.

stories.background: The city holds young people charged with serious offenses at two secure centers: Horizon in the Bronx and Crossroads in Brooklyn, both run by the Administration for Children's Services. The state comptroller's office audits how the city runs them. An earlier audit, released in April 2025, found the agency had not reported 37% of incidents at the centers to state regulators between 2019 and 2023 and that many detained youths did not get an intake interview on time. The new 69-page review looks at crowding, staffing and how long young people are held.

markets.summary: Nvidia's leadership change was the main event for stocks: its shares fell 4.3% on Thursday after Jensen Huang resigned, France 24 reported, and the Nasdaq Composite and Dow each slipped about 0.4%. The damage did not spread far. Reuters reported that other AI stocks recovered part of their losses during the day, and the New York Times said stocks were still on track for their best week in months. The other pressure is interest rates. Treasury yields, the interest the government pays to borrow, saw what MarketWatch called their biggest surge since 2022 as investors bet the Federal Reserve will keep raising rates to fight inflation. On Friday morning stock futures, which signal where the market will open, were a little lower ahead of new inflation data, according to the Wall Street Journal. concept.explanation: A Treasury yield is the annual interest rate investors earn for lending money to the U.S. government by buying its bonds. Yields rise when investors expect higher inflation or more Federal Reserve rate increases, because they demand more interest to hold a bond, and they fall when investors want safety or expect rates to come down. Bond prices move the opposite way, so a jump in yields means existing bonds lost value. The 10-year yield matters most for households because lenders use it as a guide for 30-year mortgage rates and other long-term loans; when it climbs toward 5%, as it has this week, borrowing for a home or a car tends to get more expensive, while savers earn more on new bonds and certificates of deposit.
